analysis.one_liner: Requires people earning over $1 million a year to pay at least a 30% federal tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required incomes over $1 million to pay at least a 30% federal tax rate, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2021 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a "fair share" minimum tax: anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million would pay at least 30% of that income in federal taxes, after subtracting charitable contributions. Existing income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll taxes would count toward that minimum, so the tax would only apply to high earners whose current effective rate falls below 30% — typically through deductions, low rates on investment income, or other tax preferences. The $1 million threshold would rise with inflation after 2021. The bill also called on Congress to pursue broader tax reform that closes loopholes and simplifies the system. It never moved beyond a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly: the bill says the minimum tax would cut the deficit by billions of dollars a year, borne entirely by households with incomes above $1 million. Middle- and low-income taxpayers would pay nothing, and the bill's sense-of-the-Senate section calls for broader reform to close loopholes used by the wealthy. High earners whose effective rates already exceed 30% — many salaried professionals — would pay little or nothing; the main payers would be the very wealthy who currently use deductions and low rates on investment income to pay less.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Deficit reduction; taxpayers earning under $1 million

how_it_helps.text: It imposes a minimum 30% tax rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million, so high earners using deductions, capital-gains rates, or other preferences to pay a lower effective rate would owe a top-up to reach the floor.
The bill counts payroll taxes and the alternative minimum tax toward the 30% floor, so the minimum applies to total federal tax burden, not just income tax.
The bill states its purpose as cutting the deficit by billions of dollars a year and serving as a floor on taxes for the highest-income taxpayers, pending broader reform.
The $1 million threshold is adjusted for inflation and reduced by charitable contributions, so only the very top of the income scale is affected.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million whose current federal tax rate falls below 30% — typically through deductions, lower rates on capital gains and dividends, or other tax preferences. The tax is phased in above the $1 million threshold, so it applies most heavily to the largest incomes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

drawbacks.text: A minimum tax rate on million-dollar incomes would raise the cost of investing and doing business in the U.S. for the highest earners, which opponents argue could reduce incentives for investment and risk-taking.

A minimum tax on top of the existing system adds complexity rather than replacing loopholes: the bill applies as an additional levy computed against regular tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll tax, leaving the underlying deductions and preferences it is designed to counteract fully intact.

The bill itself calls the provision only 'an interim step' and says Congress should still enact broader tax reform to repeal loopholes and simplify the system — meaning the structural problem would remain even if the floor were enacted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: a 30% floor on taxes for income over $1 million would raise billions a year from the people best able to pay, cutting the deficit without touching anyone below that threshold. The costs an honest supporter would acknowledge are the classic objections to a minimum rate: it is a rough instrument that may not distinguish well between many forms of income, and a floor that applies on top of the regular code does not fix the underlying loopholes — it just guarantees a payment, so Congress could keep adding special breaks above that floor. The bill itself concedes this by framing the provision as "an interim step" and calling for more fundamental reform it never delivered. Compared with the alternative — doing nothing, as happened here — the tax floor's drawbacks are modest.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there, with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action, until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 17, 2021 and the same day was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
The complete action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee vote, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point in the 117th Congress.
The bill never advanced past the referral stage and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so no version of the 30% minimum tax was ever voted on by the full Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The highest-earning households — those with incomes over $1 million who benefit from deductions and low rates on investment income — are better off, because the bill that would have set a 30% floor on their tax rate never received a vote. The Finance Committee's inaction protected the status quo tax treatment of the wealthiest taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households earning over $1 million a year

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a 30% minimum tax rate on incomes over $1 million.

for.name: 17 Senate cosponsors
for.role: 16 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate Independents, including Sanders, Warren, Durbin, and Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill all-Democratic support on the left flank of the caucus.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Ron Wyden, Chair)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill received no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents who caucus with Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Fund managers, hedge fund partners, and other top earners who use low capital-gains rates and other preferences to pay well below 30% would owe the new top-up tax. The bill targets exactly the gap between statutory rates and what the highest earners actually pay.
